idiom_name: Akka/Pekko classic: ActorContext.setReceiveTimeout -> ReceiveTimeout message (or ZIO/cats-effect timeout combinators)
implementation_notes: The actor runtime contains the observer: ActorContext.setReceiveTimeout(deadline) makes the mailbox itself the last-seen state - if no message arrives within the deadline the actor is handed a ReceiveTimeout message, which its receive turns into the alert, so no timestamp bookkeeping is written by hand. In effect-based stacks the same role is played by combinators over a stream of arrivals: ZIO's timeout/Schedule or cats-effect Temporal.sleep/timeout interrupt the await with a TimeoutException when nothing arrives within the window. What remains application code is the per-subject expectation and the escalation policy; the runtime owns the timer, the dispatch and the message that carries the alarm.
pitfalls: The runtime arms the deadline again only after the next message arrives, and ReceiveTimeout is delivered at most once per quiet period: after alerting, an actor that does nothing else goes deaf unless it re-arms or re-sets the timeout in the handler.

ReceiveTimeout fires on mailbox silence, not on business silence: control messages, router chatter or a scheduler's own ticks keep the actor looking alive while the business flow is dead - watch the business messages and keep control traffic off that mailbox.

setReceiveTimeout(Duration.Undefined) is the only way to disarm it, and a restart/backoff strategy that recreates the actor re-arms it silently - the silence window and the restart window can then mask each other.
On effect stacks a watchdog fiber/stream must be scoped: run it in a scope that is closed on shutdown, or it keeps alerting after the service stopped.
